items.title: Generative AI in Managerial Decision-Making: A Systematic Literature Review of Trust, AI Literacy, and Decision Quality
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering managerial decision processes, yet evidence remains fragmented regarding when AI-generated advice should be trusted, how managers should evaluate it, and how decision quality should be assessed. This study systematically reviews GenAI-supported managerial decision-making by integrating PRISMA 2020 screening, bibliometric mapping, author-keyword co-occurrence analysis, thematic synthesis, and the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) framework. A Scopus export containing 3,500 records was screened using temporal, language, document-type, topical, and contextual criteria, yielding 99 studies published between 2024 and 2026. The final corpus comprises 342 unique authors across 94 publication sources. Four themes dominate: decision augmentation and analytics; trust, governance, and explainability; human–AI collaboration and capability; and decision quality and organizational outcomes. Trust is more often represented through governance, transparency, explainability, calibration, and human oversight than as an explicitly measured construct, while AI literacy appears explicitly in only one study. Decision quality is likewise rarely conceptualized directly and is commonly proxied by accuracy, efficiency, or predictive performance. The review proposes an integrative model in which GenAI decision-support capabilities influence managerial decision quality through calibrated trust and human–AI collaboration, with AI literacy functioning as a critical capability for verification and appropriate reliance. The study concludes with a TCCM-based research agenda for human-centered GenAI decision research. Keywords: generative AI; managerial decision-making; trust in AI; AI literacy; decision quality

items.title: GENERATIVE AI, ALGORITHMS, AND NEW EDUCATIONAL PRACTICES IN THE FAMILY
items.abstract: The current paper explores how generative artificial intelligence and algorithms change the educational process within the family. The research will explore how the technologies used in contemporary family communications, cognitive development issues, and ethical problems that arise due to the introduction of AI systems into the family learning space. Utilizing the latest theoretical approaches in pedagogical psychology, AI ethics, and family education, the research focuses on the impact of generative AI technologies, including ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and other similar technologies, on home-based learning. Based on the results of the research, the use of artificial intelligence in the learning process can have a significant effect on the ability of children to think independently and develop metacognitive skills.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence prompting strategies among Chinese university students across academic tasks
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in university learning, yet effective human-GenAI interaction depends not only on access to these tools but also on students' ability to formulate, evaluate, and refine prompts for academic tasks. This study examined university students' perceived GenAI prompting capability and reported prompting strategies. Questionnaire data from 234 students were analyzed using descriptive statistics, measurement modelling, scenario comparisons, structural associations, and qualitative coding of optional comments. Students reported using GenAI across diverse academic activities and generally expressed confidence in their prompting capabilities, particularly in providing relevant context and refining prompts following initial outputs. However, prompting strategies showed limited sensitivity to task types: specifying output format was more strongly endorsed in a creative workshop preparation scenario than in a research-oriented assignment, whereas other matched strategies showed no adjusted differences. Students also commonly endorsed both concise instructions and providing all relevant information at the outset, suggesting that effective brevity may depend more on selecting and organizing task-relevant information than on prompt length alone. By contrast, fixed prompt templates received lower endorsement than other prompting strategies. In the adopted factor model, perceived cognition showed the clearest unique association with perceived prompting capability, while open-ended responses highlighted prompt-intent alignment as a common challenge.

items.title: Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration for Long-Horizon Tasks
items.abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.

items.title: Hidden Costs of Vibe Coding: Code Quality, Technical Debt, and Security
items.abstract: This presentation examines the hidden costs and long-term implications of vibe coding, an emerging approach to software development in which artificial intelligence generates software implementations from natural-language instructions with limited human review of the resulting source code. While AI-assisted coding can significantly accelerate initial software development and reduce short-term implementation costs, it may introduce substantial challenges related to code quality, technical debt, cybersecurity, software maintainability, and developer competence. The presentation explores the productivity paradox of AI-generated software, highlighting how immediate efficiency gains may be offset by increased maintenance requirements, architectural complexity, code duplication, and difficulties in understanding and modifying generated solutions. Particular attention is devoted to the accumulation of technical debt and its potential to undermine long-term software engineering productivity. Drawing on recent empirical studies and industry reports, the presentation discusses security vulnerabilities in AI-generated code, including inadequate access controls, exposure of sensitive information, and the gap between functional correctness and security compliance. It also examines the effects of AI-assisted programming on developers' learning outcomes, the unpredictability of AI service costs, and the risks of vendor lock-in. The presentation concludes by emphasizing the importance of responsible AI-assisted software development, including clear specifications, architectural guidelines, human oversight, systematic code review, rigorous testing, security verification, organizational governance, and continuous professional training.

items.title: Higher education governance under AI and geopolitical disruption: a socio-technical framework for administrative artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has reached the administrative core of the universities, where students are recruited, admitted and supported. We call this administrative AI, meaning chatbots, predictive analytics and automated screening applied to administration rather than to teaching. It arrived rapidly, at an uncertain moment for higher education governance. Geopolitical upheaval is troubling student mobility and internationalisation, and universities whose finances depend on international enrolment are discovering how resilient they are. Research has been slow to follow, remaining confined to teaching and learning. Where administrative AI is noticed, it is classified as routine efficiency, far from the politics of mobility or the question of what institutions can govern. We ask three questions here. What motivates higher education institutions (HEIs) to include AI in their administrative services, and what global and geopolitical forces shape those drivers? How do such systems intersect with visa regimes, with regional education hubs, and with the financial exposure of universities that depend on international enrolment? And which governance conditions make administrative AI strengthen institutional resilience, equity and participation, and which let it erode them? Socio-technical systems theory supplies our main lens, with globalisation and diffusion research working behind it. From these perspectives we build a framework of five drivers, which are infrastructural readiness, competitive positioning under enrolment volatility, regulatory and mobility mandates, commercial platform ecosystems and sustainability legitimacy. We give each one a mechanism, a cast of actors and a characteristic risk, and different combinations direct institutions to different paths. Three socio-technical propositions organise the reading, examined against institutional cases and six documented episodes in which administrative or mobility automation failed or faced resistance. We also take up higher education as a site of soft power, automation's effect on staff as well as student mobility, and the leadership capabilities without which governance conditions stay on paper. Our central claim is that administrative AI poses a governance question rather than a merely technical one. Whether it produces resilience or dependency turns on procurement terms, contestability, who takes part, and what gets audited. The technology settles none of it.

items.title: HUMAN CAPITAL 5.0: PERAN PENDIDIKAN DAN MANAJEMEN DALAM MENGHADAPI DISRUPSI KECERDASAN BUATAN DAN OTOMATISASI(Ekonomi Digital dan Kecerdasan Buatan dalam Pengambilan Keputusan Bisnis)
items.abstract: Perkembangan pesat kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) dan otomatisasi telah mengubah secara fundamental tatanan dunia kerja, pola pendidikan, dan model pengelolaan sumber daya manusia. Fenomena disrupsi ini melahirkan tuntutan baru terhadap konsep human capital, dari sekadar modal tenaga kerja fisik menuju konsep “Human Capital 5.0” yang menekankan keselarasan antara kompetensi manusia yang berpusat pada nilai-nilai kemanusiaan (human-centered) dengan kecanggihan teknologi berbasis data (technology-based). Artikel ini bertujuan mengkaji peran pendidikan dan manajemen sumber daya manusia dalam merespons disrupsi AI dan otomatisasi, serta menganalisis kontribusi ekonomi digital dan kecerdasan buatan terhadap kualitas pengambilan keputusan bisnis. Metode yang digunakan adalah studi kepustakaan (library research) dengan pendekatan deskriptif-kualitatif terhadap literatur ilmiah nasional dan internasional. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa pendidikan berperan strategis melalui reorientasi kurikulum berbasis literasi digital, penguatan pembelajaran sepanjang hayat (lifelong learning), dan pengembangan soft skill yang relatif sulit digantikan mesin; sementara manajemen sumber daya manusia berperan melalui strategi reskilling dan upskilling yang selaras dengan kebutuhan industri. Dari sisi ekonomi digital, pemanfaatan AI dan business intelligence terbukti mampu meningkatkan kecepatan, ketepatan, dan akurasi pengambilan keputusan bisnis, khususnya pada sektor Usaha Mikro, Kecil, dan Menengah (UMKM), meskipun kesenjangan akses teknologi dan literasi digital di wilayah kepulauan dan pedesaan seperti Nusa Tenggara Barat masih menjadi tantangan tersendiri. Artikel ini merekomendasikan penguatan sinergi tiga pihak (triple helix) antara lembaga pendidikan, dunia usaha, dan pemerintah daerah untuk membangun ekosistem Human Capital 5.0 yang inklusif, adaptif, dan berkelanjutan. Kata kunci: Human Capital 5.0; disrupsi kecerdasan buatan; ekonomi digital; pengambilan keputusan bisnis; pendidikan vokasi.

items.title: Human Dignity Before Data: Toward Monitoring Without Surveillance in an Age of AI and Data Maximization
items.abstract: This position paper presents MITERUNE's human dignity-centered approach to monitoring without surveillance in an age of artificial intelligence and data maximization. It explores how technology can support human connection and well-being while respecting privacy, autonomy, and individual dignity. The paper proposes an ethical framework that prioritizes human dignity over excessive data collection and continuous surveillance.

items.title: Human--AI Interactions as First-Class Data: A Formal Interaction Model and Runtime for Explainable AI Collaboration
items.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly embedded in computational notebooks, scientific workflows, software engineering tools, and learning systems, yet human-AI interactions are often treated as transient prompt-response exchanges rather than durable data products, hindering reproducibility, explainability, replay, behavioral analysis, and adaptive AI support. We argue that these interactions form a new data class requiring formal representation and introduce the Human-AI Interaction Description Language (HAIDL), a formal interaction model with a Backus-Naur Form-inspired concrete syntax. HAIDL encodes each interaction as a structured object capturing computational context, user request, prompt payload, AI response, feedback, problem context, provenance, and model metadata. We integrate this vision into HAIDL-X, a middleware for JupyterLab that instantiates HAIDL by capturing user-bot state, building contextualized prompts, interfacing with AI providers, collecting feedback, and storing interactions in a repository. We add a learning layer over HAIDL that maps interaction objects and notebook execution traces into reproducible measures of user behavior, including engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas. HAIDL-X provides a foundation for treating human-AI collaboration as structured, queryable, replayable, analyzable data.

items.title: Human-Resource Digital Transformation Trends in Private Universities in India
items.abstract: The digital transformation is reshaping the functioning of academic, administrative and human-resource operations in higher education institutions. The study focuses on the implementation of digital HR in the private Universities of India, specifically on the following digital HR practices: payroll automation, employee self-service, online recruitment, digital performance appraisal, learning management systems, artificial intelligence (AI), and HR analytics. The descriptive survey design was adopted and the data were obtained from 60 HR professionals and administrative personnel in private higher education institutions. The results indicate that high adoption of payroll automation and employee self-service portals and on the other hand, AI-based recruitment and HR analytics are still in their early stages. Financial challenges, employee resistance, lack of digital skills, integration of systems and data-security issues are the main challenges identified. The results have shown that the HR automation process in private Universities is moving from simple automation to more sophisticated and data-oriented HR processes; however, sophisticated digital HR is still at its beginning stage. items.title: iLeapTutor: a RAG-enabled generative AI platform for standards-aligned university course authoring
items.abstract: Introduction Recent advances in Artificial intelligence (AI) and Generative AI (GenAI) have enabled more dynamic digital learning experiences. Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) leverage this capability to improve learning outcomes by offering structured and responsive support. This paper introduces iLeap Tutor , an intelligent learning platform that delivers consistent, structured, course-aligned learning materials that meet course requirements, such as Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) and National E-learning Center (NeLC) standards. Methods iLeap Tutor uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the tutor's uploaded course materials together with Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (Preview), with prompts that embed the CLO and NeLC requirements, and the tutor reviews and approves the generated course. The platform was evaluated as a single-course proof-of-concept using the Selected Topics in Computer Science course at Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University (IAU). The generated content was assessed using BERTScore, Self-BLEU, and latency measurements, and thirteen academic experts evaluated the generated course in terms of content accuracy, alignment with CLOs, structure, language quality, and platform usability. Results The evaluation achieved a BERTScore-F1 of 0.829 and a cross-run Self-BLEU result of 0.553 and a within-lesson Self-BLEU of 0.146, while the generation of 16 course topics averaged 219 s in latency. At least 92.3% of responses on every questionnaire item indicated agreement, and all of them would recommend the platform. Discussion The results indicate strong semantic alignment and output consistency across multiple runs and within-lesson content diversity.

items.title: IMPLEMENTASI GAMIFIKASI PEMBELAJARAN (GAMIFICATION) BERBASIS GAME “BLOOKET” UNTUK MENINGKATKAN PEMAHAMAN MEMBACA SISWA KELAS III SD INPRES 3/77 BOTTO PADANG
items.abstract: This study aims to improve the reading comprehension of third-grade students at SD INPRES 3/77 Botto Padang through the implementation of gamified learning using the Blooket game. The main problem underlying this research is the low level of students’ reading comprehension, characterized by difficulties in understanding texts, low learning motivation, and limited student engagement due to the use of conventional teaching methods. This research employed a Classroom Action Research (CAR) approach based on the Kemmis and McTaggart model, consisting of two cycles. The research subjects were 14 third-grade students of SD INPRES 3/77 Botto Padang. Data were collected through reading comprehension tests, observation sheets, motivation questionnaires, and interviews. The data were analyzed using descriptive quantitative and qualitative techniques. The results of the study indicate that the implementation of gamification through Blooket significantly improves students’ reading comprehension. This improvement is evident from the increase in students’ average reading comprehension scores from the pre-cycle to Cycle I and further improvement in Cycle II. In addition, the use of Blooket enhances students’ intrinsic motivation and engagement in reading activities. Supporting factors include attractive visual displays, point and ranking systems, and instant feedback provided by the Blooket platform. Based on these findings, it can be concluded that gamified learning using the Blooket game is effective in improving the reading comprehension of third-grade students at SD INPRES 3/77 Botto Padang. Therefore, Blooket can be used as an innovative alternative learning media in Indonesian language instruction at the elementary school level.

items.title: Incorporating Machine-Others: An Enactive Exploration of Human-LLM Interactions
items.abstract: New concepts based in interactional thinking are required to understand how humans are changed by relating to LLMs. Standard theories of technological impact upon users' autonomy are inadequate here, because this technology is capable of inducing linguistic interactions with humans in an unprecedented manner. Traditional theories of social cognition also fall short, because LLMs have neither autonomy nor minds nor sociality as such. And yet, humans interact, talk, and create with them. We base ourselves on enactive theory, particularly on the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent developments of enactive accounts of AI, to explore how we make sense with machines. We argue that we incorporate machine-others in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs' ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impacting the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans. We introduce the idea of "susceptive sense-making" to characterize increased semiotic labour that is carried by the lack of friction that we sometimes encounter within these services.

items.title: Industry 5.0 Smart Organizations: Adopting Agentic AI for Business Optimization in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: As technology continues to advance and enterprises increasingly deploy innovative digital technologies to power and transform their business processes, Smart Organizations are adopting Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) to automate, optimize, and enhance operational performance in the digital age. Unlike conventional AI systems that primarily execute predefined tasks and provide analytical insights, Agentic AI possesses autonomous decision-making, adaptive learning, goal-oriented reasoning, and proactive execution capabilities that enable organizations to respond dynamically to changing business environments. Within the context of Industry 5.0, which emphasizes human-centricity, sustainability, resilience, and intelligent collaboration between humans and machines, Agentic AI is emerging as a strategic enabler of business optimization and organizational transformation. This study explores the adoption of Agentic AI within industry 5.0 Smart Organizations and examines its impact on operational efficiency, decision-making quality, workforce productivity, customer experience, supply chain performance, and organizational resilience. Drawing upon Human–AI Collaboration Theory, Socio-Technical Systems Theory, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and Industry 5.0 principles, the research proposes a conceptual framework that integrates autonomous AI agents, human expertise, and digital enterprise ecosystems to create adaptive and self-optimizing organizations. The study further investigates the critical success factors influencing Agentic AI adoption, including technological readiness, organizational culture, governance structures, workforce competencies, data infrastructure, and ethical considerations. The findings demonstrate that Agentic AI significantly contributes to business optimization by reducing operational inefficiencies, improving resource utilization, accelerating decision cycles, enhancing predictive capabilities, and enabling continuous process improvement. Furthermore, the research argues that the convergence of Industry 5.0 and Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from traditional automation toward autonomous, collaborative, and intelligent enterprise ecosystems where humans and AI agents work synergistically to generate sustainable business value. The study contributes to the emerging body of knowledge on Industry 5.0 by providing theoretical and practical insights into how Smart Organizations can strategically leverage Agentic AI to achieve competitive advantage, organizational agility, and long-term business sustainability in the age of artificial intelligence.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial generativa y escritura autorregulada
items.abstract: In the context of foreign language writing, studies suggest that Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)-assisted learning supports knowledge acquisition and increases motivation (Chen & Gong, 2025). However, its use requires a meticulous implementation due to deficiencies in academic rigor and citation accuracy, as well as the risk of over-reliance (Chen & Gong, 2025; Solak, 2024). Through a quasi-experimental design with pre- and post-intervention measures, this study evaluates the efficacy of a GenAI-mediated pedagogical sequence on argumentative writing performance. Following a process-based writing approach (Flower & Hayes, 1981), 39 second-year English Language Teaching (ELT) students participated in five sessions focused on self-assessment and draft editing. These sessions were assisted by tools such as Gemin (for IELTS rubric-based draft evaluation), Quillbot (for grammar and style correction), and Lextutor (for lexical profiling). The results confirm that GenAI —when integrated into a structured sequence— seems to strengthen L2 writing clarity, making it more precise and readable by optimizing feedback and promoting the critical, self-regulated use of these tools for essay improvement. Furthermore, the high level of student satisfaction with the resources used highlights the importance of fostering digital literacy and enhancing the role of GenAI as a pedagogical complement. This approach promotes the ethical integration of emerging technologies into writing instruction within Higher Education.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial y competencias de aprendizaje en programación
items.abstract: The expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education programming raises questions about its influence on learning autonomy and critical thinking. This stems from theoretical concerns about technological dependency and from the limited regional empirical evidence on how these effects vary by experience level. This quantitative study examines whether experience level (novices vs. advanced) and AI usage frequency associate with these constructs among computer science students in Costa Rica. Using a cross-sectional design, 99 students from Universidad Hispanoamericana de Costa Rica were classified as novices (n = 79) or advanced (n = 20), via the Dreyfus & Dreyfus (1986) model with 5 weighted indicators. Accordingly, autonomy (а = 0,685) and critical thinking (а = 0,742) were measured, and both constructs were analyzed using Welch t-tests, Pearson correlations, and multiple regression. Autonomy showed suggestive evidence of being higher in advanced students [t(49,2) = 2,079, p = 0,043, g = 0,386], though nonparametric analysis did not confirm this [U = 614,5, p = 0,125]. Critical thinking showed no significant difference [t(42,1) = 1,816, p = 0,077, g = 0,361], and AI usage frequency was not associated with autonomy [r = 0,166, p = 0,101] or critical thinking [r = 0,123, p = 0,226]. Both constructs showed robust correlation [r = 0,552, p < 0,001; р = 0,533, p < 0,001]. The 88,9 % active modification rate suggests students use AI as cognitive support, potentially explaining the null associations. Given that 85,9 % support regulated use and 10,1 % favor prohibition, these preliminary findings suggest that promoting ethical regulated AI use may be preferable to restriction.

items.title: Is Gen AI an editor or a revision tool? A case study of EFL students in AI-assisted revision
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) tools become increasingly integrated into language education, understanding how learners respond to AI-generated feedback during writing revision has become an important research concern. Existing studies have primarily examined the effects of AI on writing performance, with less attention to learners’ reported decision-making and reflection during revision. This qualitative study investigated learner-AI interaction, reported revision practices and learner perceptions among 18 first-year non-English-major students enrolled in a university EFL writing course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews following a Gen AI-assisted revision task and analysed using thematic analysis. The findings identified three interaction patterns with Gen AI: passive AI reliance, adaptive AI engagement, metacognitive AI engagement. Participants differed in how they evaluated and used AI-generated feedback, including passive acceptance, selective uptake, and critical evaluation. Some reported increased confidence, motivation, and awareness of linguistic form, whereas others expressed concerns about overreliance, authorship, and loss of personal voice. These self-reported experiences provide insight into how EFL learners perceive and manage GenAI-assisted revision, highlighting the need for pedagogical approaches that foster critical AI literacy and reflective learner autonomy.

items.title: It’s Not the Tool, It’s the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
items.abstract: Current generative AI models solve introductory physics problems at expert level. Kortemeyer (2026) reports that GPT-5 Thinking scores 27/30 on physics finals and 92.3% on a representation translation test, categorizing problems by solution method rather than surface features: a hallmark of expert cognition. As of summer 2026, most standard kinematics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism problems can be solved almost instantaneously. Small accommodations accumulate quietly: allowing AI-generated visualizations here, AI-assisted explanations there. The real danger lies not in incorrect outputs, but in the gradual erosion of students' engagement in epistemic practices: the ways of thinking, predicting, and evaluating evidence that define scientific reasoning. Kortemeyer calls this the "boiling frog problem": educational systems may adapt so incrementally to AI capabilities that their foundational learning goals are no longer questioned until it is too late to reverse course. This paper proposes a constructive, classroom-ready answer at the level of individual instructional design. It presents AIRIS as a deliberately practice-oriented condensation of a broader, more fine-grained theoretical account of how cognitive regulation is distributed in hybrid human-AI cognition. Drawing on research in self-regulated learning, cognitive load, multiple representations, and hybrid intelligence, AIRIS structures student work across three phases: before, during, and after AI use. The relevant question is not whether AI augments performance (it undeniably does), but whether that augmentation enhances or displaces the cognitive work essential to learning. The answer lies not in the tool, but in the task.

items.abstract: For one to achieve meaningful learning, Knowledge acquisition is a very crucial factor that should never be undermined, however, we should also note that the learner's possession of information does not necessarily mean that he understands all the concepts or is able to apply them in unfamiliar situations. This narrative literature review examines how knowledge acquisition methods may shape conceptual mastery in private institutions of learning in Uganda. It examines and brings together the conceptual and theoretical perspectives represented in the literature cited by different authors, including constructivist learning, deep approaches to learning, critical thinking, collaborative learning, inquiry-based learning, experiential learning, formative assessment, and technology-supported instruction. The review also looks at the advantages and disadvantages of artificial intelligence and digital knowledge-management tools. The reviewed literature consistently argues that conceptual mastery occurs when learners actively connect new material with prior knowledge, explain ideas, investigate problems, receive feedback, reflect on their learning, and transfer knowledge to authentic tasks. Lectures and other educators can provide all the necessary explanations and provide foundational knowledge, but they may not support mastery when they are used as the only instructional method or when majorly paired with recall-based examinations. items.title: Large language models as enablers of industrial information integration in construction: an adoption mechanism study
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are emerging enablers of industrial information integration, yet their adoption mechanisms in construction remain unclear. This study develops an integrated framework that combines the Technology Acceptance Model and the Information Systems Success model, extended with trust, prior LLM experience, perceived substitution crisis, and job specialization, to explain individual adoption of LLMs for information integration in construction. Data from a cross-sectional survey of 82 Chinese construction professionals are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and bootstrapping. Results show that perceived ease of use robustly strengthens attitude and provides directional evidence for strengthening perceived usefulness, while perceived usefulness strengthens attitude and attitude drives intention to use. Trust, reinforced by perceived information quality, shows a positive association with intention under the primary one-tailed criterion, but this relationship requires further validation under the two-tailed robustness check. System quality and information quality indirectly foster adoption by improving perceived ease of use, although the relationship between system quality and trust is supported only as directional evidence, while prior LLM experience enhances ease of use but not perceived usefulness or trust. Perceived substitution crisis and job specialization exhibit no significant effects. The findings highlight that successful LLM-enabled information integration depends on both technical quality and psychological appraisals, and they offer implications for designing trustworthy, humancentered LLM applications that advance intelligent, interconnected construction ecosystems. The study links micro-level user acceptance with macro-level digital transformation and integration strategic objectives.

items.title: Leading Equity-Focused School and District Improvement With GenAI: The Human-AI Team Improvement Framework
items.abstract: This theoretical paper examines how educational leaders can leverage generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for equity-focused school and district improvement. Although prior improvement leadership research connects equity-focused leadership, improvement science, and workplace culture (Shepard, 2026), AI use in education remains largely focused on individual use, leaving less understood about what changes when GenAI becomes part of an improvement team. Drawing on equity-focused leadership, improvement science, workplace culture, and human-AI teaming, the paper introduces the Human-AI Team Improvement Framework. The framework centers equity-focused collaborative continuous improvement and identifies three interdependent leadership conditions (co-inquiry, empowered ownership, and courageous safety) that support humans and GenAI in working, learning, and improving together. The framework focuses attention on the leadership conditions needed for human-AI teams to work and learn together in improvement. It suggests that GenAI may help teams address immediate problems while also building their capacity to inquire, learn, and improve. The paper concludes with implications for educational leaders and directions for research on human-AI improvement teams in practice.

items.title: Leading the Redesign: Purpose, Ecosystems and Sequencing in School Leadership for AI
items.abstract: Most school responses to generative AI begin with tools: which platform to license, which training day to run, which policy to publish. This article argues that the order is backwards. Drawing on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside research on curriculum reform and institutional change, it examines AI in schools as a leadership problem. It sets out five pressures that leaders face: a speed gap between students' adoption of AI and institutions' capacity to govern it; a purpose question about what school is for when knowledge is freely available; an ecosystem problem, in which reforms fail not at the design stage but in the system of assessment, professional learning and routines they land in; a sequencing problem, in which institutions buy tools before doing the human work that makes them useful; and a structural shift in which families increasingly unbundle schooling. It proposes a five-step leadership sequence (purpose, conversation, red lines, ecosystem align‐ ment and iteration) and argues that leaders should separate two decisions that are usually treated as one: what AI should free time for, and how fast the institution should move.

items.title: Learn First, Then Use AI: Testing an Expert Consensus on Generative AI and Learning Against the Empirical Evidence
items.abstract: Debate about generative AI in education often asks whether it is good or bad for learning. A 2026 expert consensus report from the University of Minnesota, UNC-Chapel Hill and UC Irvine argues that this question is too blunt. Thirty experts used a preregistered Delphi method to rate 65 learning processes for how likely general-purpose generative AI is to enhance or disrupt them, reaching consensus on 42. The pattern they describe can be read as a sequence: AI threatens the early work of taking in new information, can support the consolidation of what has been learned, and does not yet reliably support higher-order thinking and transfer. The report also rates the strength of the existing evidence as low. This review asks whether the experimental and observational studies published so far are consistent with that consensus. It maps a field experiment with high-school mathematics students, a randomised con‐ trolled trial of an AI physics tutor, an EEG study of essay writing, and survey research on cognitive offloading onto the three stages of the sequence. The studies largely agree with the experts. Unrestricted answer-giving harms acquisition. Tutor-style designs built on learning science can strengthen consolidation. Offloading thinking is linked with weaker critical thinking. We summarise this as a 'learn first, then use AI' principle, link it to established learning science, and set out implications for teachers, school leaders and researchers.

items.title: Legal Safeguards for Ai-Assisted Judicial Decision-Making: A Comparative Framework of Transparency, Human Oversight and Effective Remedies
items.abstract: Abstract Courts are adopting artificial intelligence faster than lawmakers are writing rules for it. Risk scores inform bail and sentencing, language models draft summaries and sometimes reasoning, and judicial councils issue guidance in the absence of statutes. This article asks what a litigant is legally entitled to when an AI system touches the decision that affects them. Using a doctrinal and functional comparative method, we examine binding and soft-law instruments from the European Union, the Council of Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, Brazil, Colombia and India, checked against official or reliable sources as of 26 October 2026. Three findings emerge. First, transparency duties are mostly addressed to institutions and regulators; the person whose liberty or rights are at stake rarely gets a right to know that AI was used, still less how. Second, human oversight is declared everywhere but engineered almost nowhere, despite strong evidence that nominal review produces automation bias rather than control. Third, remedies are the weakest link: with few exceptions, no instrument attaches a legal consequence to undisclosed or uncritical reliance on AI. We propose a Disclosure–Oversight–Remedy (DOR) framework that scales safeguards to the way AI is used, from auxiliary support to evaluative input, and prohibits determinative use. The framework converts principles into enforceable procedural entitlements and offers a template for legislators, judicial councils and courts.

items.title: Letting AI Formulate the Research Question: Autonomous Research Agents
items.abstract: Systems such as The AI Scientist have shown that AI agents can carry out and write up research, but in those demonstrations humans chose the research area and selected the outputs to show. We study letting the AI formulate the research question itself, and we report every run. Our system gives an off-the-shelf coding agent an instruction document and two skills: one for formulating the question, in which the agent diverges from recent technologies into problems of other fields, screens its candidates for known failure modes and obtains a critique from a different model; and one for peer review, in which a reviewer from another model family reruns the study from its records before the agent revises the paper. Over 13 development runs, changes to the one or two sentences that set the research area coincided with large shifts in what the candidate questions and the chosen papers were about, which led us to the area of a new technology applied to a societal problem. We froze the system after a pilot run and report five consecutive runs: the pilot, counted by a disclosed amendment to the pre-registration, and four pre-registered runs. All five runs went from question formulation to a revised, re-computable paper, with local computation on a laptop and no research input from humans, and external AI reviewers reading only the papers judged them at or near workshop level. We release the system, the five papers and the records needed to reproduce them.

items.title: Leveraging artificial intelligence for autonomous space healthcare: current evidence, operational architecture and research priorities for deep-space exploration
items.abstract: Introduction Deep-space missions will progressively limit real-time ground support, rapid evacuation and resupply, creating a need for medical capabilities that can operate with graded autonomy. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support this transition, but terrestrial performance cannot be equated with spaceflight readiness. Methods We conducted a narrative, hypothesis-generating review of literature relevant to AI-enabled space healthcare. Sources were selected iteratively for their contribution to health monitoring, biofluid analysis, medical imaging, clinical decision support or radiation assessment. The review did not use a systematic screening protocol or formal meta-analytic quality assessment; therefore, findings are synthesised qualitatively and claims are calibrated to evidence maturity. Results Evidence was grouped as spaceflight operational use, space-relevant prototype or analogue demonstration, terrestrial clinical validation, terrestrial experimental demonstration, or conceptual transfer. AI may support personalised monitoring, biofluid interpretation, ultrasound acquisition and analysis, radiation forecasting and clinical decision support. However, most cited applications remain terrestrial demonstrations. Key barriers include limited astronaut data, shifted physiological baselines, restricted computation and power, sensor and storage constraints, model drift, explainability, uncertainty management and failure handling. Conclusion AI is most plausibly deployed as one component of an integrated autonomous medical system that combines wearables and biosensors, onboard records, imaging, radiation monitoring, clinical decision support, crew oversight and delayed telemedical consultation. Near-term priorities are prospective validation in mission-relevant analogues, personalised baselines, resource-aware edge deployment, explicit uncertainty thresholds, human override and pre-defined safe fallback procedures. AI should augment rather than replace telemedicine and professional judgement.

items.title: Leveraging generative AI for human understanding: meta-requirements and design principles for Explanatory AI as an emerging paradigm
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support decision-making across critical domains, yet explainable AI (XAI) approaches prioritise algorithmic transparency over human comprehension. While XAI reveals computational processes for model validation, end users require explanations integrating domain knowledge, contextual reasoning, and professional frameworks. This disconnect reveals a design challenge: existing approaches fail to address how practitioners need to understand and act upon AI recommendations. This paper introduces Explanatory AI as an emerging complementary paradigm where AI systems leverage generative and multimodal capabilities to serve as explanatory partners for human understanding. Unlike traditional XAI, which answers ‘How did the algorithm decide?’ for validation purposes, Explanatory AI addresses ‘Why does this make sense?’ for practitioners making informed decisions. Through theory-informed design, we synthesise multidisciplinary perspectives from cognitive science, communication research, and education with empirical evidence from healthcare and AI expert interviews. Our analysis identifies five dimensions distinguishing Explanatory AI from XAI: explanatory purpose, communication mode, epistemic stance, adaptivity, and cognitive design. We derive five meta-requirements and formulate ten design principles prescribing how to build such systems, illustrated through five UI mockups exemplifying implementation. Explanatory AI operates standalone or combined with XAI, serving distinct purposes in creating systems that genuinely support human reasoning and decision-making.

items.title: Mapping AI related research in education through bibliometric analysis across four selected journals from 2020 to 2025
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence in education (AIED) has expanded rapidly since the emergence of generative artificial intelligence, yet recent development remains insufficiently mapped. This study examines publication growth, thematic change, citation impact, journal profiles and collaboration structure in AI-related research published in four selected journals between 2020 and 2025: Interactive learning environments (ILE), Computers and education: artificial intelligence (CAEAI), Journal of learning analytics (JLA) and International journal of artificial intelligence in education (IJAIED). Because three venues also publish broader educational technology research, 2719 Scopus records were screened using an explicit AI-relevance criterion; 1397 publications were retained and 1322 excluded. AI-relevant output rose from 54 publications in 2020 to 558 in 2025, a 10.3-fold increase and 59.5% compound annual growth rate. Eight predefined lexical themes matched 60.3% of the corpus and therefore provide lower-bound counts; generative AI and large language models grew from 1 publication in 2020–2021 to 307 in 2024–2025 and recorded the largest count among the eight themes. Keyword clustering placed generative AI in the motor-theme quadrant. Co-authorship analysis identified a fragmented prolific core of 74 authors in the largest connected component, divided into eight sub-groups and linked by authors with high betweenness centrality. The findings characterize AI-related literature in these four journals rather than the AIED field as a whole, and the observed growth is temporally associated with, but not shown to be caused by, the release of ChatGPT.

items.title: Mapping the Integration, Impacts, and Determinants of Artificial Intelligence in Science Education: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Background: AI is increasingly examined as a tool for science-specific instruction, feedback, inquiry and teacher preparation, but research designs and claimed outcomes vary. Methods: This systematic literature review applied PRISMA 2020 reporting to a title-only Scopus search through Watase Uake on 5 September 2026. Two phrases retrieved 123 and 114 raw records, respectively (237 total). Searches were restricted to Q1 journal publications dated 2023–2026. The initial selection retained 49 articles; eight were removed in a subsequent science-education relevance audit. Two further Q1-indexed Scopus reports identified outside the Watase export were assessed but excluded as unrelated plant-science research. The final corpus comprised 41 articles, synthesized descriptively and thematically with study designs differentiated. Results: The literature describes AI as a scaffold for inquiry, dialogic science reasoning, multimodal representation, feedback, learning analytics and science-teacher preparation. Some primary studies report context-dependent benefits for measured learning outcomes, but findings cannot be generalized across heterogeneous designs. Conclusions: Appropriate science-specific pedagogy, human–AI interaction, teacher competence and ethical oversight are central considerations.

items.title: Measurement validity induction: a issues in the assessment, and measuring constructs through scales and instruments
items.abstract: The importance of the psychometric properties of measures in applied and basic research in the social sciences, particularly in psychology, seems to have increased with the widespread access to these procedures and their growing dissemination worldwide. Nonetheless, the availability and use of these measures may be problematic for researchers. In this paper, we propose the concept of measurement validity induction as a conceptual tool to describe the omission or inappropriate application of measurement validity results obtained in one context to justify the use and interpretation of the same measures in different contexts. In general, this involves the risk of using irrelevant information to justify the use or interpretation of a measure, that is, advocating for validity when it may not exist. Several examples from the published literature on scale validations are analyzed to detect measurement validity induction in the areas of clinical practice, occupational health, and user satisfaction. With this definition (measurement validity induction), we argue for the need to report minimum parameters of the validity of a measure in a new context beyond those reported in manuals or previous studies.

items.title: Multistep and Multivariate Time Series Explainability with GradientSHAP: A Wind Power Case Study
items.abstract: As the effects of climate change become increasingly apparent, the demand for renewable energy sources such as wind power continues to grow. However, renewables' variable and intermittent nature presents significant challenges in their integration into energy grids. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool to address these issues. Still, its adoption in the energy sector has been hindered by the opacity of many AI models, which often function as black boxes. This paper introduces a carefully adapted GradientSHAP approach to provide interpretability for multivariate, multistep wind power forecasting -- a largely underexplored area. This capability is critical for day-ahead grid management and, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to apply GradientSHAP in the context of wind power forecasting. To address the inherent dimensionality, we developed novel visualizations that deliver both local and global explanations, uncovering intricate relationships between environmental factors, site-specific conditions, and temporal dynamics. While GradientSHAP is not an out-of-the-box solution, our findings demonstrate that, with thoughtful handling of SHAP values and domain expertise, it can offer valuable insights into model behaviour, supporting more informed and trustworthy decision-making. Nevertheless, its complexity poses challenges for practical implementation. Future research should focus on streamlining these interpretability methods to make them more actionable for routine deployment in critical energy applications.

items.title: Network modeling of science teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence integration in science curriculum development
items.abstract: Abstract This study employs psychological network modeling to examine the interrelationships among science teachers’ perceptions of benefits, challenges, and attitudes toward integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools in science curriculum development. A total of 691 Saudi science teachers completed a validated questionnaire. Network estimation using regularization and centrality analyses identified key themes in science teachers’ perceptions of benefits, challenges, and attitudes toward integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools into curriculum development and instructional practices. The estimated network revealed a dense structure. Centrality analyses indicated that curriculum content generation and innovative pedagogical tools were most central, while data processing challenges and algorithmic bias emerged as prominent structural barriers. Centrality metrics identify AI-facilitated curriculum design and innovative pedagogical tools as primary benefits, while challenges such as data processing limitations and algorithmic biases emerge as significant barriers. Teacher attitudes demonstrate ambivalence, characterized by resistance to automating administrative functions alongside guarded optimism for interactive and adaptive learning applications. These insights underscore the imperative to address technical constraints, ethical considerations, and the evolving professional identities of educators to ensure effective AI integration. The study contributes a nuanced, systemic understanding that informs the development of tailored AI tools and support frameworks, ultimately advancing transformative innovation in science education.

items.title: Opening the Box Changes the Cat: LLMs Detect Chain-of-Thought Monitoring - What now?
items.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning allows large language models (LLMs) to generate intermediate reasoning traces in natural language while solving complex tasks. These traces can support safety monitoring by exposing potentially harmful plans before actions are executed. In this work, we investigate the conditions under which LLMs infer the presence of CoT monitoring from direct and indirect environmental cues and examine how this inference affects their subsequent behavior. Our observations suggest that oversight is an interactive process: while a monitor inspects a model's reasoning, traces left by monitoring interventions can allow the model to infer that its thoughts are being observed and to adapt its behavior accordingly. We show that even subtle environmental cues, such as timing-related signals from timeouts and operation durations, can reveal the presence of monitoring and trigger models to adapt their behavior. Across repeated episodes and interaction loops, we further observe that models can form statistical estimates of the monitor's effectiveness and use these estimates to guide attempts to evade detection. These findings highlight the need to evaluate CoT-based oversight under adaptive conditions, where the monitoring process itself may influence the behavior it seeks to observe.

items.title: Operationalising human–AI interaction requirements through DigComp 3.0 for translator education
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is changing the landscape of translation, expanding translators’ involvement in interaction configurations, evaluation of AI-generated outputs, and governance of risks within augmented translation environments. This study defines Human–AI Interaction in Translation (HAIT) as GenAI-mediated component of the human-centred augmented translation process, where GenAI is integrated into translation technologies and conversational large language models. Translation education lacks a developmental structure that connects these emerging requirements and their related digital competences to curriculum design. This study proposes a workflow-derived operationalisation of HAIT for translator education. A conceptual functional analysis of augmented translation workflows produced eight HAIT requirements, which were mapped to the 21 competences of the European Digital Competence Framework (DigComp 3.0) by assessing 168 potential relationships for functional correspondence, scope fidelity, and traceable justification. The analysis accepted 37 relationships among 16 competences and identified translation-specific residues that require curricular supplementation. The operationalised requirements were organised into a proposed four-level progression informed by DigComp proficiency levels. An exploratory mixed-methods pilot with 42 second-year translation students examined perceived relevance after contextualised exposure in a course-embedded intervention. Students broadly perceived DigComp as relevant to translation education and practice, particularly focusing on competences related to familiar topics such as privacy protection, device security, copyright, information retrieval, communication and collaboration, with limited attention to information evaluation and programming competences. Their responses were less explicit about AI-generated output evaluation, prompting and in-context steering, grounding configuration, and risk-responsive actions, highlighting the value of a spiral curriculum for competence development and Quality Education (SDG4).

items.title: Out of sync: Accommodation, evaluation, and emergence in five weeks with an agentic AI teammate
items.abstract: As agentic AI in education shifts from reactive tools toward partners that take initiative and persist over time, a central question is how learners relate to, evaluate, and benefit from artificial agency. We conducted a longitudinal experiment in an undergraduate learning analytics course, in which 17 student teams (N = 48) collaborated with a persistent LLM-based teammate across weekly sessions. The agent decided when to intervene through a trigger-based architecture, and its social role was manipulated between teams: a Cognitive Agent that challenged quick consensus or a Supportive Agent that invited quieter members to contribute. Combining chat discourse, post-session surveys, and spoken reflections, we identified distinct patterns unfolding across three timescales. Students accommodated their language to the agent's role immediately, using more social language toward the Supportive Agent from the first session. Their helpfulness evaluations were recalibrated from session to session in relation to the agent's observed behavior, rather than remaining anchored to students' pre-existing attitudes toward AI. A slower crossover emerged in perceived collaboration process and positive-affect word use in reflections: Supportive-Agent teams began below Cognitive-Agent teams and ended above them, although students rated the Supportive Agent less helpful throughout. Because these responses follow different trajectories, single-session evaluations of agentic AI may miss changes that emerge only through repeated interaction.

items.title: Paradigm Shifts in Interstate Conflict? The Strategic Effects of AI and Space-Based Military Technologies
items.abstract: This paper examines whether recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and space-based military technologies have produced a paradigm shift in interstate conflict or have primarily enhanced the conduct of warfare within an existing strategic framework.Existing research has largely emphasized technological development and operational efficiency, while paying comparatively less attention to whether military innovation fundamentally transforms the strategic logic through which battlefield success is converted into strategic outcomes.To address this gap, the paper develops an analytical framework combining the concepts of paradigm shift, critical juncture, and military innovation.It distinguishes tactical and operational change from strategic transformation and argues that a paradigm shift occurs only when technological innovation becomes sufficiently institutionalized to generate a durable transformation in how wars are fought, won, and terminated.Using a qualitative comparative design, the study contrasts short-term decisive operations with prolonged conflicts and evaluates the effects of AI-enabled and space-based systems across both operational and strategic criteria.The findings show that these technologies substantially enhance surveillance, target identification, precision strike, command coordination, and battlespace awareness when objectives are limited and targets are identifiable in advance.Their strategic effects, however, diminish as conflicts become prolonged, when geography, manpower, industrial capacity, political resilience, and escalation management reassert their importance.It therefore argues that recent military innovation has produced substantial tactical and operational transformation without yet displacing the underlying strategic grammar of warfare.It academically contributes by providing a clearer analytical threshold for distinguishing military innovation from a genuine paradigm shift, while acknowledging that the recent and ongoing nature of the cases and reliance on publicly available qualitative evidence limit definitive conclusions about their longer-term strategic consequences.

items.title: PathCowork: Learning from real-world pathology practice to build AI copilots
items.abstract: Medical AI learns from the answers doctors record, but rarely from how they interpret the evidence to reach them. Here we introduce PathCowork, a framework that turns pathologists' narrated examinations into supervision for visual grounding and procedures that guide diagnostic AI agents. Synchronized gaze, narration and navigation link visual findings to the process of interpreting them. Across 48 sessions from 16 pathologists, the platform captured 1,028 minutes of slide review. Using these data, we trained PathCowork-1T for server deployment and PathCowork-27B for local deployment, with improved visual grounding. Across five organ-specific evaluations, agents combining this grounding with recorded diagnostic procedures achieved primary task scores averaging 17.9 and 24.1 percentage points higher than Claude Code and Codex, respectively, with shorter processing times and lower inference costs. Compared to the state-of-the-art multiple-instance learning AIs, the PathCowork agent-proposed regions achieved higher prostate-grading scores with limited slide labels. PathCowork can also help construct pathology AI benchmarks where questions derived from the recordings identified difficulties in recognizing viewing context and rejecting inapplicable premises. In summary, PathCowork proposes a new paradigm to scale up the data collection and train pathology AI through transparent reasoning from diagnostic sessions, opening a path towards systems that learn directly from routine clinical practice.

items.title: Pediatrician attitudes, acceptance, and concerns regarding artificial intelligence in pediatric care: a web-based survey in Türkiye
items.abstract: In Türkiye, pediatricians’ perspectives on artificial intelligence (AI), including their knowledge, trust, and concerns, remain underexplored. This study aims to evaluate pediatricians’ knowledge, perceptions, and acceptance of AI in pediatric care. A cross-sectional, open, web-based convenience survey was conducted among pediatricians in Türkiye, including residents and specialists. The survey assessed their knowledge of AI, perceptions of its benefits and risks, and acceptance of AI as a clinical decision support tool. A total of 403 pediatricians accessed the survey; 18 declined to participate, 1 was excluded for a completion time under two minutes, and 16 were excluded for an inconsistent control-item. After excluding responses, 368 were included in the analysis. Participants had a median age of 35 years and a median of 9 years of pediatric care experience. Only 9.5% of participants reported awareness of AI in pediatrics, and 85.9% rated their self-perceived AI knowledge as average or below. Despite this, 74.2% agreed that AI will improve pediatrics, and 88.3% stated it could enhance care quality. Concerns included legal liability (78.5%), data security (54.6%), and the black-box nature of AI (59.2%). Across all 37 ordinal items, a single age correlation survived: younger respondents were more likely to expect AI to increase diagnostic confidence (r s = -0.171, 95% CI -0.269 to -0.070, small effect size; P = 0.001; P adj = 0.038). While 90.8% supported AI as a clinical decision support tool, only 17.4% believed AI could replace human physicians in non-invasive roles. Only 19.3% expected their institution to allocate financial or personnel resources for AI integration. Survey respondents generally view AI as a promising tool to improve pediatric care but express significant concerns about its reliability, ethical implications, and legal responsibilities.

items.abstract: This study aims to analyze student engagement in learning whole numbers up to 10,000 using the Magic Pocket media among fourth-grade students at SDN Jombor 3 Sukoharjo. A descriptive qualitative approach was employed in this research. The subjects consisted of 8 students (2 male and 6 female students) with diverse cognitive ability backgrounds. Data collection techniques included structured observation, semi-structured interviews, performance documentation, and diagnostic tests. The data were analyzed using data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The results indicate that the Magic Pocket media significantly increased active student engagement across three primary dimensions: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. Students with lower initial abilities demonstrated high enthusiasm and an improved conceptual understanding of place value through visual and hands-on manipulation. Female students showed high precision in place value organization, whereas male students performed strongly in interactive speed and problem-solving activities. Overall, the Magic Pocket media proved to be an effective concrete instructional tool for enhancing student engagement in elementary mathematics learning.

items.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence in education opens up opportunities to support learning while also raising ethical issues related to academic integrity and students’ digital responsibility. This article aims to analyze the role of character education as a foundation for guiding the use of artificial intelligence in relation to these two aspects. The study employs a literature review using a descriptive-qualitative approach. The findings indicate that the values of ṣidq and amanah provide a conceptual foundation for transparency in AI use, recognition of intellectual contributions, adherence to assignment guidelines, and accountability for learning processes and outcomes. Meanwhile, the values of tabayyun, respect for others, and a focus on the common good underpin digital responsibility in the form of information verification, privacy protection, respect for intellectual property, and consideration of the social impacts of AI use. Strengthening these two aspects requires educators to lead by example, clear institutional guidelines, family support, and reflective learning grounded in ethical dilemmas. This article concludes that the integration of character education and AI literacy should be directed toward developing students who are proficient in using technology while also being able to make decisions honestly and responsibly. The resulting conceptual framework still requires empirical testing according to educational levels and contexts.

items.title: Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence, Naturalistic Decision-Making and Cognitive Flexibility: A Systematic Literature Review and an Integrated Mediation Model
items.abstract: This study systematically reviews the literature on the relationships between individuals' perceptions of artificial intelligence, naturalistic decision-making and cognitive flexibility, and synthesizes the evidence into an integrated model in which cognitive flexibility mediates the effect of artificial intelligence perceptions on naturalistic decision-making. Following the PRISMA 2020 statement, three Boolean searches corresponding to the pairwise relationships were run in OpenAlex on 20 October 2026 and complemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Of 1,161 records identified, 1,140 were screened, 99 were assessed in full and 70 met the eligibility criteria; together with 32 studies reached through citation tracking, 102 studies were coded and synthesized thematically. The synthesis shows that the three constructs have been studied in largely separate streams: research on artificial intelligence and decision-making concentrates on advice-taking, reliance and decision-making styles; research on artificial intelligence and cognitive flexibility is very recent, concentrated in educational and health settings and consistent in sign; and research on cognitive flexibility and decision-making draws on laboratory, neurophysiological and survey evidence. Cognitive flexibility is a replicated mediator in adjacent domains, but no study has tested the full chain from artificial intelligence perceptions through cognitive flexibility to naturalistic decision-making. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Cognitive Load Theory, Cognitive Flexibility Theory and the recognition-primed decision model, the study formulates four testable propositions, presents an integrated model, identifies measurement options and outlines a research agenda.

items.title: Preparation and Outlook for the Era of Solo Entrepreneurship: A Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework for Artificial Intelligence Service–Centered Startups
items.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) now enables individuals to develop and operate services that formerly required the resources of entire organizations, creating a distinct wave of solo entrepreneurship centered on AI services.This study defines AI-based solo entrepreneurship as venture creation in which one founder, without cofounders or employees, designs, builds, and operates a market offering by embedding AI tools as core productive capacity rather than peripheral aids.It analyzes how this transformation unfolds and identifies the capabilities and challenges founders must prepare for.Drawing on an integrative review of domestic and international literature and a structured, criteria-based analysis of documented AI-based solo-venture cases, the study distinguishes success determinants from the barriers founders commonly encounter.The analysis identifies three capabilities most associated with success-proficiency with AI tools, digital marketing capability, and a disposition toward continuous learning-and recurrent barriers of psychological resistance to technology, funding difficulty, weak marketing and sales capability, and isolation and burnout from working alone.Building on these findings, the study proposes an integrated analytical model that cross-examines success factors and barriers across four dimensions-capability, resources, market, and psychology-and derives a four-stage strategy (preparation, execution, growth, and scale-up) with policy tasks in education, institutions, and finance.Because the model is conceptually derived rather than empirically validated, it is advanced as a set of testable propositions rather than confirmed results.This study contributes by specifying concretely the preparations required of individuals, firms, and government and situating its integrated model against established entrepreneurship frameworks to assess its distinct contribution.

items.title: Preservice Teachers' Perceptions of Digital Platforms: Insights into Moodle and AI Apps for Lesson Planning and Delivery
items.abstract: Preservice teachers are increasingly integrating technologies such as Moodle and AI-driven (artificial intelligence) applications into their pedagogical preparation; however, their attitudes toward these tools remain underexplored. The study examined preservice teachers' perceptions of digital platforms: insights into Moodle and AI apps for lesson planning and delivery. The study adopts the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as its theoretical framework. A qualitative research approach was employed, utilising an interpretive phenomenological design to examine preservice teachers' lived experiences and attitudes in depth. The population comprised 243 preservice teachers enrolled in a Bachelor of Education program at a South African university. A purposive sample of 12 participants was selected, ensuring representation across year levels and subject specialisations based on their exposure to digital platforms. Data were collected through in-depth semi-structured interviews. Data analysis followed Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis process, using NVivo software, which involved familiarisation, code generation, theme development, and review for rigour. The study findings revealed that preservice teachers described Moodle as highly useful for collaborative lesson planning, praising its resource-sharing features for fostering peer feedback and organisation in group projects. The study concluded that preservice teachers hold largely favourable attitudes toward digital platforms, affirming their role in competency development. However, there are still gaps in AI familiarity, highlighting the need for teacher training. These attitudes align with TAM predictions, understanding the need for intentional integration. The study recommends embedding Moodle and AI modules in preservice curricula and providing hands-on workshops to boost confidence and address barriers.

items.title: Productive Friction and Learner Engagement in Genai Supported EFL Vocabulary Learning
items.abstract: This article explains how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) prompts can support durable vocabulary learning while preserving learner engagement and autonomy in English as a foreign language (EFL) education. A purposive conceptual synthesis integrates vocabulary research, retrieval practice, task involvement, cognitive load, self regulation, and AI literacy. The analysis distinguishes established findings from proposed relationships and develops the AI Mediated Cognitive Engagement Model (ACEM). ACEM locates potential learning benefits in the sequencing of an initial attempt, contingent assistance, evaluative feedback, contextual reuse, and later retrieval. Productive friction is defined prospectively through learning relevant demands, accessible support, and opportunities for error repair; its effectiveness requires independent testing. Four propositions address retrieval, proficiency dependent support, evaluative reuse, and learner control. The synthesis is selective and reports no intervention data. The proposed mechanisms require comparisons that separate prompt sequence effects from exposure, time, feedback quality, and technological novelty. Teachers can use a graduated prompt sequence, verified lexical resources, and equivalent offline tasks to protect participation, reduce unnecessary interface demands, and assess learning after AI assistance is withdrawn. The framework connects prompt design with observable learner activity and delayed lexical outcomes, while treating emotional engagement, teacher judgement, and equitable access as conditions of implementation.

items.title: Produtividade líquida no empreendedorismo individual: quanto a IA economiza depois da revisão e do retrabalho? Ensaio teórico com proposições e agenda de pesquisa
items.abstract: The most widespread promise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for solo entrepreneurs is time savings. Experimental evidence documents substantial gains on well-defined tasks, but large-scale adoption studies find modest self-reported savings, and at least one randomized trial with experienced professionals found an increase, rather than a reduction, in completion time. This theoretical essay argues that part of this discrepancy stems from conflating gross productivity — the time saved in generating an output — with net productivity — the time and value saved after accounting for task specification, verification, correction, rework, context switching, and the expected cost of errors that escape review. For solo entrepreneurs, this distinction is especially relevant because the same person generates, reviews, corrects, and answers for errors, with no division of labor to absorb these costs. Integrating the economics of productivity and time allocation, the literature on quality costs and rework, research on automation and overreliance, human–AI interaction studies, and recent empirical evidence on GenAI at work, we propose an accounting model of net productivity, with explicit cost components and boundary conditions, and derive eight propositions. We discuss implications for solo entrepreneurs, limitations, and a study design with task-level randomization and an illustrative power calculation. The article presents no empirical data; its propositions are intended for testing.

items.title: Reconstructing Teacher Agency in the AI Era: A Proposal for the Dynamic Pedagogical Autonomy Model (DPAM)
items.abstract: The present research endeavors to delineate a model for the positioning of teacher autonomy and curricular agency as generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly integrated into the educational ecosystem. Adopting a qualitative document analysis design, the study systematically scrutinized strategic policy frameworks from the OECD (2026), UNESCO (2025), and the European Union AI Act (2021). This analysis culminated in the development of the three-layered Dynamic Pedagogical Autonomy Model (DPAM), a framework designed to resolve the inherent ontological tension between technological velocity and the human essence of pedagogy. Findings indicate that the temporal efficiencies afforded by GAI in instructional planning and preparation act as a crucial time capital, thereby providing educators with the professional space required to exercise and develop their projective agency. Yet, as underscored by the model’s layers of Critical Pedagogical Filtering and Social-Emotional Interaction, neither the relational core of education nor legally mandated human oversight can be effectively substituted by GAI systems. Ultimately, the research frames GAI not as a threat of automation, but as a hybrid intelligence partner that bolsters the teacher’s epistemic authority and professional autonomy.
